records.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
records.author: codekarate
records.storyText:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

https://factory.mastra.ai

https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

records.title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
records.author: atugard
records.storyText:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here.

It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it.

I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome.

Thanks, David

records.title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests
records.author: atomarch
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses.

The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right.

The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome.

kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

records.title: Show HN: KradleBench – Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft
records.author: jamest
records.storyText:
Hi HN -

This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you!

Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds.

1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property.

2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies.

3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too.

Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety.

Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals.

We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens.

Thanks for reading,

James & Kemal

records.title: Show HN: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB
records.author: leetheguy
records.storyText:
Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents.

That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months.

It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup.

I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees.

The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them.

This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far)

I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups.

- Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

records.author: tniich
records.storyText:
Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine.

Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work.

The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots:

- caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed

- local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2

- draw on screen during calls or before screenshots

- AI agents monitoring

- AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh)

We built it because of two things:

1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them.

2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel.

This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass).

Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.

records.title: Show HN: ToolJet 4.0 – vibe-code internal tools with governance
records.author: kriztle
records.storyText:
Founder here, I posted the beta version of ToolJet on HN in 2021 as a no-code/low-code builder. Ended up getting 400 upvotes.

I wrote the first version in 7 weeks during the covid lockdown, and the drag and drop builder was the whole product. Over the last few months our customers wanted the UI flexibility and convenience of vibe coding without giving up the governance they came to ToolJet for. We resisted for a while.

We did not pivot, but we did rebuild the app builder so an app can be built with code or without it. The frontend of apps is a React codebase, written by Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or by hand, and ToolJet is the platform it runs on.

How it works: - Internal tools can be generated using your own coding agents or using our agent.

- Frontend is React codebase, it can be edited from our app builder, VS code, or any other IDE.Code will be scanned for security issues before saving. Scanning policies can be set by admins.

- Frontend never interacts with APIs, databases or other data sources. Every interaction with data source goes through our backend where we enforce access control. We have 100+ data source integrations.

- Platform comes with version, environment and release management.

- Changes can be reviewed visually as well before promoting to prod. Workflows can be setup to have reviewers and reviews/approvals.

- Platform handles SSO, RBAC and more granular access control.

Would love to hear where this breaks for you.

I created Globus, to stay informed about the world.

The app was born out of frustration with how ignorant I was getting about the world outside of the media bubble. It was true when I lived in Norway, and the ignorance got to a whole other level after moving to the US.

Globus publishes one edition per day, 20 to 30 stories, laid out on a globe. It lets us see places that rarely make it into the news cycle, simply because there's only so much room for the navelgazing stories that usually saturate our media diet.

Spin the globe freely to browse, tap a story for a short summary, and dive into background information and original reporting if you are curious. Done. No doomscrolling.

The app is ad-free, and every story is open for the first 7 days, with no account or subscription needed. After that, $4/month or $30/year.

I’m still refining the story selection and the app itself, so I’d love honest feedback about what works, what feels off, and what’s confusing. And what kind of stories you'd like to see.

And I freely admit that Globus feels like "the bad news app" some days, so better surfacing of stories that offer a semblance of hope and inspiration will be an ongoing priority.

records.title: Show HN: Intrusive.ai – open-source AI attack simulation
records.author: tomhavoc
records.storyText:
I created the INTRUSIVE.AI platform to give agent builders the ability to evaluate their agents against OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (and more generally, just to allow for comprehensive testing in a non-production environment).

Through my own experience with evaluating agents, I found indirect prompt injection testing to be especially difficult due to the architectural nature of it. To overcome that challenge, I created Interceptor Sandbox - a sandbox that runs agents in a simulated environment where all of the services an agent might rely on (HTTP, MCP, Postgres/pgvector to name a few) can be "intercepted" via an injection API to inject malicious payloads.

Interceptor Sandbox: https://github.com/intrusiveai/interceptor_sandbox

Additionally, I found that existing open source AI testing and attack simulation solutions didn't provide the breadth of capabilities I needed so I created Attack Harness for that purpose. But it also had to be sandboxed because any sufficiently capable attack harness can't be trusted to play nice once it's been given nefarious goals and so that led to Operator Sandbox. I haven't seen other people talking about the sandboxing method that I've employed in Operator so it seems to be a somewhat novel approach that might shake up the way people are thinking about sandboxing AI agents.

Operator Sandbox: https://github.com/intrusiveai/operator_sandbox

The full suite is documented here: https://docs.intrusive.ai

The platform is still very much in its alpha stage so your mileage may vary but I would sure appreciate any feedback that comes my way. Feel free to use GitHub Issues on the respective repos to provide feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Klistra – A complete studio for spec-driven AI motion design and video
records.author: pvarghav
records.storyText:
As a solo-dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. Note that this was before AI-coded music videos went viral, back in the early days when the models were just getting good enough to make the result actually look good.

In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow into an easy to use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, web scraper and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. This way there is always a written specification that matches the render / build. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one time packs (Pro starting at $25/mo and packs at $12). Being a solo-dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

I created tutorials covering the basics. Mostly relying on the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic and for advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

You can see demo videos on the home page https://klistra.ai/ and on the tutorial pages. I would love to see what you make!

Some additional notes:

- After feedback from friends there is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Klistra can create images too.

Happy to hear what you think!

records.title: Show HN: Run CalculiX, OpenFOAM and ParaView jobs on your office's idle PCs
records.author: dmitrat
records.storyText:
OmnibusCloud aims to join different user devices into a single computing engine, which I call the Ultracomputer. Today it works with Windows, Linux, or Mac OS (ARM) computers. Next, it will be able to connect smartphones, tablets, game consoles, and any other computing device.

It is no secret that most of our computers spend most of their lives idle, and there have been attempts to use this idle power before. The most famous of them is BOINC. But OmnibusCloud, following the first part of its name, is trying to provide a system that will be easy to use for any actors.

OmnibusCloud is splitting tasks into chunks and distributing them to machines available to you. Each machine processes its own chunk individually and then sends back the result.

Today, OmnibusCloud is introducing simulation tools:

- ParaView plugin allows users to render engineering animations, similar to render farms like SheepIt does for Blender, on machines in your group

- PrePoMax solver replacement can distribute thermal analysis tasks to machines in your group

- WitSweep can plan and run hundreds of FEA (with CalculiX solver) or CFD (with OpenFOAM solver) cases in one click; you can schedule your research that will start on your office machines when everyone is at home, and then in the morning you will get the results.

OmnibusCloud works on a crowdcomputing model, similar to crowdfunding, but with computer power instead of money. The one who needs computation can open a project, and users can join it.

Today we are just launching the public beta, so there are very few users and machines, so to try our system, it will be better to start with a Private Group. Create your own group and invite your friends or team (or connect your office workstation) - you will get your own subnetwork to run your tasks.

Check our repositories: https://github.com/OmnibusCloud

You will find there public controllers and integrations with some applications (they are published with an MIT license) that you can use as an example to build your own controller or integration to solve your own tasks.

records.title: Show HN: Topothesy – a daily online geography game
records.author: proy87
records.storyText:
I'm not very good at geography and don't know the exact locations of many cities. That's why it is hard for me to play games where you have to pin cities precisely on a map.

But what if you place cities relative to other cities?

That's how idea of a puzzle was born: given a set of cities, choose any five and place them correctly relative to other on a 5x5 grid. The topmost city is the northernmost, the leftmost is the westernmost. There should be only one city in each row and column, since the cities are not strictly vertical or horizontal relative to each other.

The goal of the game is to try to find the most compact set of cities. If cities are far from each other, it is quite easy to place them; on the other hand such set will be far from compact. It is much harder to find a compact set and to place it correctly.

The main challenge in developing the game was to make it moderately difficult. It is quite easy to place Los Angeles and Sydney, but much harder to place Osaka and Kyoto. Another issue is to make it interesting every day: it is not interesting to place Zurich, Milan and Marseille too often.

So, I want to ask:

1. Are the rules clear? Have you encountered some difficulties?

2. Is the game interesting? Is it too hard or too easy?

3. I feel that it can be used for learning, but I don't know how. Any ideas?

Thank you very much in advance.

The puzzle is available here: https://www.topothesy.com

You just send a message to Confetti's WhatsApp account, the occasion, who is it for, and you will get a link from which your friends can join, and send their clip. When everything is ready you will get the final video, with all of the clips stitched together.

The free version is one video of up to 3 minutes with everyone in it; premium is CHF 2.99 once per video for the full length, HD, and names (more to come). Feel free to test it, and tell me if you like the flow, if the price is fair, or anything else you'd like to get off your mind.

records.title: Show HN: Goldcrest, a household financial model you fill in by talking
records.author: tralfamadorian8
records.storyText:
I built Goldcrest in Toronto for my own use in the hope it helps others. I've been discussing a rent vs buy scenario with my partner and found that it requires a surprising number of variables and complexity to do proper modelling/forecasting (the model implementation is a Monte-Carlo simulation under the hood). I then extended it to financial planning since most of the groundwork was already built from the rent vs buy model.

I did look at some other financial planning tools and noticed that the main difference between all other tools and my workflow was that I was primarily interfacing with an LLM to discuss, learn, plan, and build my models vs filling out form inputs (rather tediously). So, I thought that could be something that other people would like to do as well. Most of my friends aren't in software, and if they use LLMs it's for fairly basic things. For me at least, it's easier to type into a chat, "Hey, I make $x/year, have a wife and kids, a house valued at $x, a TFSA/Roth IRA with $x, etc." Right now I have the chat agent prompting the user. It's a similar experience to how one might have a conversation with a financial advisor, however with slightly more guardrails (e.g. the LLM never does math, just translates your input to form inputs).

The other tedious aspect of financial planning that I unfortunately can't solve right now is financial data integrations (investment platforms, banks, etc). So users have to collect their financials on their own for now.

I also wanted to put an emphasis on privacy given my personal detest for companies that don't value it, so everything is pseudonymized (similar to anonymization).

The model leverages open-source data to ensure everyone (well, USA and Canada at the moment) has a tailored forecast that calculates in-depth tax considerations for various registered investment accounts, full-time vs self-employed income, detailed future expense considerations and "events" like having a child or selling a house, Social Security/CPP/OAS, etc. Everything is also manually reviewable and configurable for users inclined to do so. I'm working on an educational aspect/feature so users can ask the LLM questions. I also have plans to expose an MCP for power users so you can hook-in with your own LLM.

There's also a Sankey diagram for income breakdown. Everyone loves a Sankey diagram.

Thanks for reading.

I'd love to hear your thoughts and feedback.
